patterns.name: Cross-Government API Gateway
patterns.description: Standard approach for exposing APIs to other government departments through the central gateway.
patterns.problem: Departments need to share APIs securely but managing individual connections is complex and inconsistent.
patterns.solution: Route all cross-department API traffic through the Government API Gateway, which handles authentication, rate limiting, and monitoring centrally.
consequences: Consistent rate limiting and quota management
Single point of visibility for cross-government traffic
Requires gateway team for onboarding new APIs
patterns.diagram:
graph LR
    A[Consuming Service] --> B[API Gateway]
    B --> C[Auth Service]
    B --> D[Rate Limiter]
    B --> E[Provider API]
    E --> F[Backend Service]

codeExample.description: Registering an API with the gateway

patterns.name: Event-Driven Cross-Department Integration
patterns.description: Using asynchronous events for non-time-critical data sharing between departments.
patterns.problem: Synchronous API calls create tight coupling and cascading failures when services are unavailable.
patterns.solution: Publish domain events to a shared event bus. Consuming departments subscribe to relevant events and process them asynchronously.
consequences: Eventually consistent data (not suitable for real-time)
patterns.diagram:
graph LR
    A[Producer] --> B[Event Bus]
    B --> C[Consumer 1]
    B --> D[Consumer 2]
    B --> E[Consumer 3]
    subgraph DCS
    C
    end
    subgraph RTS
    D
    end
    subgraph NHDS

    end

patterns.name: Cross-Department Data Sharing
patterns.description: Framework for establishing and managing data sharing agreements between departments.
patterns.problem: Sharing data across departments requires legal agreements, technical contracts, and ongoing governance.
patterns.solution: Standardised data sharing agreement template with automated technical contract generation and access auditing.
consequences: Reduces time to establish new sharing arrangements
Requires upfront investment in governance processes

patterns.name: OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials Flow
patterns.description: Standard authentication pattern for service-to-service communication within government.
patterns.problem: Services need to authenticate with each other securely without user involvement.
patterns.solution: Use OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with short-lived tokens and scope-based access control.

codeExample.description: Obtaining and using an access token

patterns.name: Mutual TLS for Sensitive APIs
patterns.description: Using client certificates for highly sensitive service-to-service communication.
patterns.problem: Some APIs require stronger authentication than tokens alone, especially for sensitive data.
patterns.solution: Require client certificates (mTLS) in addition to OAuth tokens for sensitive API access.

patterns.name: Centralised Secrets Management
patterns.description: Pattern for managing API keys, certificates, and credentials across government services.
patterns.problem: Services need secure access to credentials without hardcoding or manual distribution.
patterns.solution: Use Government Secrets Manager (Vault-based) with dynamic credentials and automatic rotation.
consequences: No secrets in code or config files

codeExample.description: Retrieving secrets from the secrets manager

patterns.name: Citizen Consent Management
patterns.description: Pattern for managing citizen consent for data sharing between services and departments.
patterns.problem: Citizens must consent to data sharing, and services need to verify consent before accessing data.
patterns.solution: Centralised consent service with fine-grained permissions. APIs check consent before returning data.
consequences: Citizens can view and revoke consent
Additional API call for consent checking

patterns.name: Data Minimisation in APIs
patterns.description: Returning only the minimum data required for the consuming service's purpose.
patterns.problem: APIs often return more data than consumers need, creating unnecessary data exposure.
patterns.solution: Design APIs with purpose-specific endpoints that return only required fields. Use scopes to control data access.
consequences: May require multiple endpoints for different purposes

patterns.name: Security Audit Logging
patterns.description: Comprehensive logging of security-relevant events for compliance and investigation.
patterns.problem: Security incidents and data access must be traceable for compliance and forensics.
patterns.solution: Structured audit logs with correlation IDs, sent to centralised log aggregation with tamper protection.
consequences: Must not log sensitive data values

patterns.name: Circuit Breaker Pattern
patterns.description: Preventing cascading failures when downstream services are unavailable.
patterns.problem: When a downstream service fails, repeated calls waste resources and can cascade failures.
patterns.solution: Implement circuit breakers that open after failures, return fast failures, and periodically retry.

patterns.name: API Rate Limiting Strategy
patterns.description: Protecting APIs from overload while ensuring fair access for all consumers.
patterns.problem: APIs can be overwhelmed by excessive requests, affecting all consumers.
patterns.solution: Implement tiered rate limits at the gateway based on consumer classification and API sensitivity.

patterns.name: Asynchronous Notification Pattern
patterns.description: Sending citizen notifications without blocking the main request flow.
patterns.problem: Notification delivery (email, SMS) is slow and can fail; blocking on it degrades user experience.
patterns.solution: Queue notification requests for asynchronous processing. Use callbacks or polling for delivery status.

patterns.name: Webhook Best Practices
patterns.description: Reliable webhook delivery for event notifications to external systems.
patterns.problem: Webhooks can fail due to network issues or consumer downtime, leading to lost events.
patterns.solution: Implement retries with exponential backoff, signature verification, and idempotency.

patterns.name: Identity Proofing Levels
patterns.description: Framework for establishing identity confidence based on evidence strength.
patterns.problem: Different services require different levels of identity confidence, but there's no consistent framework.
patterns.solution: Define identity proofing levels (low, medium, high) with specific evidence requirements for each.
consequences: Services can specify required confidence level
Higher levels require more user effort

patterns.name: Biometric Liveness Detection
patterns.description: Ensuring biometric samples are from a live person, not a photo or replay attack.
patterns.problem: Biometric systems can be fooled by photos, videos, or masks without liveness checks.
patterns.solution: Implement active or passive liveness detection as part of biometric capture and verification.

patterns.name: Idempotent API Operations
patterns.description: Ensuring API operations can be safely retried without duplicate effects.
patterns.problem: Network failures can cause clients to retry requests, potentially causing duplicate transactions.
patterns.solution: Require idempotency keys for mutating operations. Store and check keys before processing.

patterns.name: Business Rules Engine Pattern
patterns.description: Externalising complex business rules from application code for easier updates.
patterns.problem: Eligibility and calculation rules change frequently; embedding them in code requires deployments.
patterns.solution: Use a rules engine with version-controlled rule definitions that can be updated independently.

patterns.name: FHIR Resource Patterns
patterns.description: Using HL7 FHIR standards for health data interoperability.
patterns.problem: Health data is exchanged in many formats, making integration complex and error-prone.
patterns.solution: Adopt FHIR R4 as the standard for health data APIs, using standard resources and profiles.
consequences: Rich ecosystem of tools and libraries

patterns.name: Accessible Form Design
patterns.description: Building forms that meet WCAG 2.1 AA and work for all users.
patterns.problem: Forms are often inaccessible to users with disabilities, failing legal requirements.
patterns.solution: Use design system components with built-in accessibility. Follow GOV.UK form patterns.
consequences: Works for all users including assistive tech

policies.name: Net Zero Digital Infrastructure
policies.description: Mandates that all government digital services measure and reduce their carbon footprint. Requires departments to report on data centre energy usage, optimize cloud workloads, and preference green hosting providers.
objectives: Reduce government digital carbon emissions by 50% by 2030
Mandate green hosting for new services
Require carbon reporting for all APIs with >1M monthly requests
Establish cross-government green cloud procurement framework

policies.name: Cross-Government Data Sharing Framework
policies.description: Establishes the legal basis and technical standards for sharing citizen data between government departments. Requires explicit consent management, audit trails, and standardised APIs for all inter-departmental data exchanges.
objectives: Enable secure data sharing while protecting citizen privacy
Reduce duplicate data collection across departments
Establish common data standards and APIs
Implement consent management across all citizen services

policies.name: Government Digital Identity Programme
policies.description: Creates a unified approach to verifying citizen identity across government services. Mandates adoption of GOV.UK One Login for all citizen-facing services, with provisions for high-assurance identity proofing where required.
objectives: Single sign-on for all government services
Reduce identity fraud in public services
Eliminate redundant identity checks between departments
Support multiple identity verification levels (low/medium/high)

policies.name: Welfare Data Integration Reform
policies.description: Streamlines benefit eligibility checking by enabling real-time data sharing between DCS (benefits), RTS (income), and NHDS (health). Aims to reduce assessment times and eliminate the need for citizens to provide the same information multiple times.
objectives: Reduce benefit assessment time from weeks to days
Automate income verification for 80% of claims
Enable health data sharing for disability assessments (with consent)
Create single view of citizen circumstances across departments

policies.name: Secure by Design Framework
policies.description: Mandates NCSC security principles for all government digital services. Requires threat modelling, security testing, and continuous monitoring as part of service development and operation.
objectives: Embed security in all stages of service development
Achieve Cyber Essentials Plus for all public-facing services
Implement zero trust architecture across government
Establish shared security operations capability
